title: Special Senses: Vision, Hearing, Balance, Taste, and Smell
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)

overview.intro: This chapter follows each special sense from its receptor to the cortex: the visual pathway and the pupil, phototransduction, the fluids and glands that keep the eye working, hearing, balance, taste, and smell. Board questions rarely ask for a pathway in isolation. They give a field defect, a pupil exam, a tuning fork result, a direction of nystagmus, or a lost sense after head trauma and ask you to name the lesion and explain the finding. Each of these answers comes from knowing where fibers cross or converge, which ion carries the receptor current, and how the two sides of the brain are compared.
prerequisites: G protein coupled receptor signaling and second messengers (cAMP, cGMP, IP3)
Resting membrane potential and the Nernst equation, especially for K+
Brainstem and thalamic nuclei and the cortical lobes (NE-3)
Cranial nerve nuclei, ganglia, and foramina (NE-8)
Parasympathetic and sympathetic outflow to the head (NE-9)

connections.how: Facial nerve lesions at different levels change tearing, taste, and the stapedius reflex, so the special senses localize a CN VII injury.

connections.to: CNS blood supply (NE-10) and vascular disease (NE-20-A)
connections.how: Middle and posterior cerebral artery strokes produce the quadrantanopias and macular sparing hemianopia described here.
Vitamin A supplies the retinal of rhodopsin, so deficiency causes night blindness before it damages the cornea.
Pituitary adenomas and craniopharyngiomas reach the optic chiasm and announce themselves with bitemporal field loss.
Glaucoma, presbycusis, Meniere disease, and benign paroxysmal positional vertigo are disorders of the normal mechanisms taught in this chapter.

terms.def: Loss of the same half of the visual field (right or left) in both eyes, produced by any complete lesion behind the optic chiasm.
Loss of one quarter of the visual field, usually homonymous, from a partial lesion of the optic radiations.
A weaker pupillary response to light shone in one eye than in the other, caused by asymmetric optic nerve or severe retinal disease.
Pupils that constrict for near focus but poorly or not at all to light.
The G protein cascade by which light absorbed in a photoreceptor closes cGMP-gated cation channels and hyperpolarizes the cell.
The steady inward cation current through open cGMP-gated channels that keeps photoreceptors depolarized in darkness.
The positive potential of about +80 mV in the K+-rich endolymph of the scala media, generated by the stria vascularis.
The orderly mapping of sound frequency to place, high frequencies at the cochlear base and low frequencies at the apex, kept throughout the auditory pathway.
Hearing loss from failure to carry sound through the external or middle ear to the cochlea.
Hearing loss from damage to cochlear hair cells, the cochlear nerve, or its central connections.
A three-neuron brainstem reflex that moves the eyes opposite to head rotation by an equal amount, keeping the image stable on the retina.
Rhythmic eye movement with a slow drift in one direction and a corrective fast phase in the other, named by the direction of the fast phase.

sections.title: The visual pathway and visual field defects

blocks.text: The lens projects an inverted, left-right reversed image onto the retina. The temporal visual field therefore falls on the nasal retina, and the upper field falls on the lower retina. Retinal ganglion cell axons leave the eye at the optic disc as the optic nerve, a CNS tract wrapped in meninges.

At the optic chiasm, above the pituitary gland, fibers from the nasal half of each retina cross and temporal fibers stay on the same side. Each optic tract therefore carries the opposite half of the visual world from both eyes, which is why every complete lesion behind the chiasm produces a homonymous defect, while a lesion in front of it affects one eye only.

Most tract fibers synapse in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus, which keeps the two eyes in separate layers; a minority leave the tract before the LGN for the pretectal area (pupillary reflex, C02) and the superior colliculus. From the LGN the optic radiations fan back to the primary visual cortex on the banks of the calcarine sulcus. Fibers from the lower retina, which carry the upper field, loop forward around the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle in the temporal lobe (the Meyer loop) and end on the lower bank (lingual gyrus). Fibers from the upper retina, carrying the lower field, run through the parietal lobe to the upper bank (cuneus).

The macula, which serves central vision, is represented at the occipital pole. The posterior cerebral artery (PCA) supplies the calcarine cortex, but the pole often receives collateral flow from the middle cerebral artery (MCA). A PCA infarct therefore commonly spares central vision, whereas an optic tract lesion cannot. A pituitary adenoma presses on the chiasm from below, so it injures the inferior crossing fibers first and the upper temporal fields go first; a craniopharyngioma presses from above and tends to take the lower temporal fields first.

blocks.title: Lesion site and visual field defect (lesions on the right side)
rows: Optic neuritis, ischemic optic neuropathy, trauma
Blind right eye; right relative afferent pupillary defect
MCA stroke, temporal tumor or surgery
Left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
blocks.caption: In front of the chiasm defects are monocular, at it heteronymous, and behind it homonymous. Lateral chiasm pressure catches uncrossed temporal fibers.

blocks.title: Worked example: localizing a field defect
blocks.text: A 46-year-old woman bumps into door frames on both sides. Confrontation testing shows loss of the temporal half of the field in each eye, worse above. Step 1: both eyes are affected, so the lesion is at or behind the chiasm. Step 2: the defects are on opposite sides of the world in the two eyes (heteronymous), and only the crossing nasal fibers serve both temporal fields, so the lesion is at the chiasm. Step 3: upper fields come from the inferior retina, and inferior nasal fibers cross in the lower chiasm, so the compression comes from below. The likely cause is a pituitary macroadenoma growing upward out of the sella.

blocks.predict: A patient has a left homonymous hemianopia with central vision preserved. Where is the lesion, and which artery is involved?
blocks.explain: Homonymous loss places the lesion behind the right chiasm, and macular sparing points to the occipital cortex, where the pole has collateral supply from the MCA when the PCA is occluded.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on the macula and the last two rows of the table.

sections.title: Pupillary light reflex, accommodation, and abnormal pupils

blocks.text: Pupil size is set by two muscles of the iris. The sphincter pupillae constricts the pupil (miosis) under parasympathetic control through muscarinic receptors; the dilator pupillae widens it (mydriasis) under sympathetic control through alpha-1 receptors. The sympathetic route has three neurons: hypothalamus to the ciliospinal center at about C8 to T2, then to the superior cervical ganglion, then along the internal carotid artery and the long ciliary nerves.

blocks.title: Pupillary light reflex
steps: Light activates retinal ganglion cells
Axons run in optic nerve, chiasm, and tract
Fibers bypass the LGN to the pretectal nucleus
Each pretectal nucleus projects to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei
Preganglionic fibers travel in CN III to the ciliary ganglion
Short ciliary nerves contract both sphincter pupillae
blocks.caption: Afferent limb CN II, efferent limb CN III. Bilateral pretectal projections make direct and consensual responses equal.

blocks.text: The near response (accommodation reflex) has three parts: convergence by the medial recti, pupillary constriction, and a rounder lens. The ciliary muscle, a parasympathetic target of the same CN III pathway, contracts and moves the ciliary body forward and inward, slackening the zonular fibers so the elastic lens rounds up and increases its refractive power. The near response is driven from the visual cortex and reaches the oculomotor complex by a route that does not pass through the pretectal nucleus, which explains why light and near responses can be separated by disease.

Because the efferent signal always goes to both eyes, an afferent lesion cannot make the pupils unequal. Unilateral optic nerve disease shows instead as a relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil): on the swinging flashlight test both pupils constrict when the normal eye is lit, then both dilate when the light swings to the affected eye, because that eye sends a weaker signal. A dense cataract does not cause it, since scattered light still reaches the retina.

Anisocoria (unequal pupils) therefore points to an efferent problem or a normal variant. Comparing the pupils in bright and dim light tells which pupil is abnormal. Pupillary fibers run on the outer surface of CN III and are supplied by pial vessels, so a compressive lesion (posterior communicating artery aneurysm, uncal herniation) dilates the pupil early, whereas diabetic ischemia of the nerve core usually spares it.

blocks.title: Interpreting abnormal pupils
rows: Small difference, about 1 mm or less, similar in light and dark; normal reactions
Small pupil, difference greater in the dark; mild ptosis; anhidrosis with proximal lesions
Large poorly reactive pupil, difference greater in bright light; ptosis; eye down and out
Asymmetric optic nerve or severe retinal disease
Equal pupils at rest; both dilate when light swings to the affected eye
Dorsal midbrain lesion near the pretectal area, classically neurosyphilis
Small, irregular, usually bilateral; constrict to near but not to light
blocks.caption: A larger difference in the dark means the small pupil is abnormal; a larger difference in bright light means the large pupil is abnormal.

blocks.text: The Argyll Robertson pupil is the classic light-near dissociation. A lesion near the pretectal area interrupts the light pathway to the Edinger-Westphal nucleus while sparing the more ventral near response fibers. Light-near dissociation also occurs with dorsal midbrain compression (Parinaud syndrome) and with a tonic (Adie) pupil, but those pupils are typically large.

blocks.predict: The swinging flashlight test shows both pupils dilating whenever the light reaches the left eye. Are the pupils equal at rest, and where is the lesion?
blocks.explain: Yes, because each pretectal nucleus drives both Edinger-Westphal nuclei. A weaker afferent signal from the left optic nerve or severely diseased left retina gives a left relative afferent pupillary defect.
blocks.check: Compare with the light reflex flow and the paragraph on the swinging flashlight test.

sections.title: Phototransduction in rods and cones and vitamin A

blocks.text: Photoreceptors work in reverse of most receptors: they are depolarized in the dark and hyperpolarize to light. In darkness, a high concentration of cGMP in the outer segment holds cGMP-gated cation channels open. Na+ and Ca2+ flow in (the dark current) while Na+-K+ ATPase in the inner segment pumps Na+ out. The cell rests near -40 mV and releases glutamate continuously from its synaptic terminal.

Rhodopsin, the rod pigment, is a G protein coupled receptor made of the protein opsin bound to 11-cis retinal, an aldehyde of vitamin A. A photon isomerizes 11-cis retinal to all-trans retinal, which changes the shape of opsin into its active form (metarhodopsin II).

blocks.title: Phototransduction in a rod
steps: Photon converts 11-cis retinal to all-trans retinal
Activated rhodopsin activates the G protein transducin
Transducin alpha-GTP activates cGMP phosphodiesterase
Phosphodiesterase hydrolyzes cGMP; cGMP falls
cGMP-gated Na+ and Ca2+ channels close
Rod hyperpolarizes toward about -70 mV
Glutamate release onto bipolar cells falls
blocks.caption: Each step multiplies the signal: one activated rhodopsin activates many transducins, and each phosphodiesterase destroys many cGMP molecules, so a rod can respond to a single photon.

blocks.text: Less glutamate is itself the signal. Bipolar cells with metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR6) are inhibited by glutamate, so they depolarize when light arrives (ON pathway); those with ionotropic receptors hyperpolarize (OFF pathway). Splitting the signal this way lets the retina report both increases and decreases in light.

The response is switched off by rhodopsin kinase and arrestin, which inactivate rhodopsin, and by the intrinsic GTPase of transducin. Closing the channels also lowers intracellular Ca2+, which relieves Ca2+ inhibition of guanylyl cyclase, so cGMP is resynthesized; this negative feedback underlies light adaptation. In dark adaptation, sensitivity rises over about 20 to 30 minutes as bleached pigment is regenerated.

Bleached all-trans retinal is reduced to all-trans retinol, carried to the retinal pigment epithelium, isomerized back to the 11-cis form, and returned to the photoreceptors. This visual cycle needs a steady supply of vitamin A from the blood. Rods carry dim-light vision and depend almost entirely on rhodopsin, so vitamin A deficiency first appears as night blindness (nyctalopia). Vitamin A, acting through retinoic acid, also maintains specialized epithelia, so prolonged deficiency adds keratinizing metaplasia of the conjunctiva and cornea: xerophthalmia, Bitot spots, and finally keratomalacia.

blocks.title: Rods compared with cones
rows: Rhodopsin, one type, peak about 500 nm
Three photopsins, peaks about 420 (S), 530 (M), and 560 (L) nm
Peripheral retina; absent from the central fovea
Low, near one to one at the fovea: sharp acuity
blocks.caption: Both use the same cascade; they differ in pigment, sensitivity, location, and wiring.

sections.title: Aqueous humor and the tear film

blocks.text: The cornea and lens have no blood vessels, so aqueous humor supplies their nutrients and removes their wastes. It is formed by the ciliary processes at about 2 to 3 microliters per minute. Plasma filters out of fenestrated capillaries in the ciliary stroma, and the nonpigmented ciliary epithelium then secretes Na+, Cl-, and HCO3- into the posterior chamber, with water following osmotically. Na+-K+ ATPase powers the Na+ transport, and carbonic anhydrase supplies the HCO3-, which is why both enzymes are control points for secretion. Beta-adrenergic stimulation raises secretion through cAMP.

Aqueous flows from the posterior chamber through the pupil into the anterior chamber and leaves at the iridocorneal angle. Most passes through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm, a circular endothelial channel that drains through collector channels to the episcleral veins. A smaller share leaves by the uveoscleral route through the ciliary muscle. Intraocular pressure, normally about 10 to 21 mmHg, is set by the balance between secretion and outflow resistance, and the trabecular meshwork supplies most of that resistance.

Glaucoma is optic neuropathy, usually with raised pressure, in which ganglion cell axons are lost at the optic disc, producing cupping and peripheral field loss first. In open-angle glaucoma the angle is anatomically open but trabecular resistance rises slowly, so loss is painless and gradual. In angle-closure glaucoma the peripheral iris is pushed against the trabecular meshwork. A shallow anterior chamber (often a small hyperopic eye or a thickened lens) and a mid-dilated pupil increase contact between iris and lens, aqueous builds up behind the iris, and the iris bows forward and seals the angle; pressure then rises sharply with pain, redness, and blurred vision.

The tear film keeps the cornea smooth, moist, and protected. Each layer has its own source, so the cause of dry eye can be predicted from which source fails. Tears spread with each blink and drain through the puncta, canaliculi, lacrimal sac, and nasolacrimal duct into the inferior meatus of the nose.

blocks.title: Layers of the tear film
rows: Meibomian glands in the tarsal plates
Slows evaporation; dysfunction gives evaporative dry eye
Lacrimal gland and accessory lacrimal glands
Volume, lysozyme, lactoferrin, and IgA; loss gives aqueous-deficient dry eye (for example Sjogren syndrome)
Lets the watery layer wet the corneal surface; lost when goblet cells are lost (vitamin A deficiency, scarring)
blocks.caption: Modern descriptions merge the aqueous and mucin layers into one gel, but the three sources still predict the type of dry eye.

blocks.title: Parasympathetic pathway to the lacrimal gland
steps: Superior salivatory nucleus in the pons
Nervus intermedius of CN VII
Through the geniculate ganglion without synapse
Greater petrosal nerve, then nerve of the pterygoid canal
Synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion
Postganglionic fibers ride V2 and V1 branches to the gland
blocks.caption: Reflex tearing uses corneal afferents in CN V1 and this CN VII efferent pathway.

blocks.text: The flow localizes facial nerve injury. A lesion at or proximal to the geniculate ganglion, as with a skull base fracture or a cerebellopontine angle tumor, removes tearing and gives a dry eye. A lesion at the stylomastoid foramen, as in typical Bell palsy, spares the greater petrosal nerve, so tear secretion is preserved; the eye still waters because a weak orbicularis oculi fails to close the lids and pump tears into the drainage system.

sections.title: Hearing: sound conduction, hair cell transduction, and hearing tests

blocks.text: Sound in air would mostly reflect off the higher-impedance fluid of the inner ear, and the middle ear overcomes this mismatch. The tympanic membrane has about 17 times the effective area of the stapes footplate, and the lever action of the ossicles adds about 1.3 times more, so pressure at the oval window is raised about 20 times. The stapedius (CN VII) and tensor tympani (CN V3) damp loud sound, so a facial nerve lesion can cause hyperacusis.

The scala vestibuli and scala tympani contain perilymph, which resembles extracellular fluid (high Na+, low K+) and connects at the apex through the helicotrema. Between them, the scala media holds endolymph, with K+ near 150 mmol/L and an endocochlear potential of about +80 mV, both produced by the stria vascularis. The organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane, with the stereocilia of its hair cells touching the overlying tectorial membrane.

blocks.title: Sound transduction
steps: Sound vibrates the tympanic membrane
Ossicles drive the stapes into the oval window
Traveling wave peaks at one place on the basilar membrane
Stereocilia shear against the tectorial membrane
Tip links open channels; K+ enters from endolymph
Hair cell depolarizes; Ca2+ entry releases glutamate
Spiral ganglion neurons fire into CN VIII
blocks.caption: The round window bulges outward as the stapes pushes in, letting the fluid move.

blocks.text: Hair cell transduction uses K+ rather than Na+. Bending the stereocilia toward the tallest row stretches tip links and opens mechanotransduction channels at their tips. The driving force for K+ entry is the sum of the +80 mV endocochlear potential and the negative hair cell interior, about 150 mV in total, so a large current flows at little metabolic cost to the hair cell, and K+ leaves basolaterally into low-K+ perilymph. Inner hair cells, about 3,500 in number, receive about 90 to 95% of the afferent fibers and are the true sensory cells. Outer hair cells, about 12,000, change length with voltage through the motor protein prestin and amplify basilar membrane motion; they are the most vulnerable to noise and ototoxic drugs.

Tonotopy follows the mechanics of the basilar membrane. Near the oval window (base) it is narrow and stiff and resonates with high frequencies; toward the apex it is wide and flexible and responds to low frequencies. The normal range is about 20 to 20,000 Hz. Noise and aging (presbycusis) damage the base first, so high frequencies are lost first. Centrally, CN VIII reaches the cochlear nuclei, then both superior olivary nuclei, the lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus, medial geniculate nucleus, and the primary auditory cortex (Heschl gyrus, superior temporal gyrus). Above the cochlear nuclei each ear is represented on both sides, so unilateral deafness means a lesion of the ear, CN VIII, or cochlear nucleus, not of the cortex.

blocks.title: Weber and Rinne tests (512 Hz tuning fork)
rows: Air louder than bone; both reduced
blocks.caption: Rinne asks whether the middle ear is working; Weber shows which cochlea is working better.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading the tuning forks
blocks.text: Muffled hearing in the left ear; Weber lateralizes left. That fits a left conductive or a right sensorineural loss, and Rinne decides. On the left, bone is louder than air, so sound is not crossing the left middle ear: left conductive loss (cerumen, middle ear effusion, otosclerosis). Weber goes to the worse ear because bone-conducted sound reaches both cochleae equally, but the blocked ear is shielded from room noise and loses less energy out through the canal, so its intact cochlea hears it louder. Had Rinne been positive on the left with Weber going right, the loss would be left sensorineural.

sections.title: Vestibular system, the vestibulo-ocular reflex, vertigo, and motion sickness

blocks.text: Vestibular hair cells carry a bundle of stereocilia and one tall kinocilium. Bending toward the kinocilium depolarizes the cell and raises the firing rate of its afferent above a steady resting rate; bending away hyperpolarizes it and lowers the rate. Because each nerve fires at rest, each side reports motion as a change from baseline, and the brain reads head movement from the difference between the two labyrinths.

blocks.title: Vestibular end organs
rows: Crista in the ampulla, capped by a gelatinous cupula
Angular acceleration (head rotation) in the plane of the canal
Macula, roughly horizontal, with calcium carbonate otoconia
Horizontal linear acceleration and head tilt
blocks.caption: The canals lie at about right angles and work in push-pull pairs; turning to the left excites the left horizontal canal and inhibits the right.

blocks.text: When the head starts to turn, endolymph lags behind the duct by inertia and deflects the cupula. The cupula has the same density as endolymph, so gravity does not move it, and during steady rotation the fluid catches up and the signal fades; on stopping, the fluid keeps moving and the opposite rotation is felt. Otoconia are denser than endolymph, so the otolith membrane slides under linear forces and gravity, which lets the maculae signal head tilt.

blocks.title: Horizontal vestibulo-ocular reflex (head turns left)
steps: Left horizontal canal excited, right canal inhibited
Left vestibular nuclei fire more
Signal crosses to the right abducens nucleus
Right lateral rectus contracts
Via the medial longitudinal fasciculus, left medial rectus contracts
Both eyes move right, keeping the image stable
blocks.caption: A three-neuron arc (vestibular ganglion, vestibular nucleus, ocular motor nucleus) gives the reflex a very short latency.

blocks.text: If one labyrinth or vestibular nerve fails suddenly, as in vestibular neuritis, the intact side's resting input is no longer balanced and is read as continuous rotation toward the intact side. The result is vertigo (an illusion of movement), nausea, and spontaneous nystagmus. The VOR drives the slow phase toward the damaged side, and a corrective saccade gives the fast phase away from it. Peripheral nystagmus beats in one direction and is suppressed by visual fixation; nystagmus that is purely vertical, changes direction with gaze, or is not suppressed suggests a brainstem or cerebellar lesion.

Caloric testing uses the same logic. With the horizontal canal brought vertical, cold water in one ear sets up convection that inhibits that canal, mimicking a turn to the opposite side, so the fast phase beats away from the cold ear; warm water does the reverse (COWS: cold opposite, warm same). In benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, loose otoconia in a canal, usually the posterior one, move with gravity and deflect the cupula, so brief vertigo follows changes in head position. In Meniere disease, excess endolymph (hydrops) causes episodic vertigo with fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus, and fullness.

Motion sickness arises when vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive signals disagree, for example reading in a moving car, where the eyes report stillness while the labyrinth reports motion. Vestibular nuclei and the cerebellar nodulus relay the mismatch to brainstem vomiting circuits; histamine H1 and muscarinic receptors in these relays carry the signal, which explains the drowsiness and nausea that accompany it.

blocks.predict: A patient has sudden vertigo from a left vestibular neuritis. Which way does the fast phase of the nystagmus beat, and toward which side does the patient tend to fall?
blocks.explain: The intact right side dominates, so the brain senses rotation to the right. The slow phase drifts left and the fast phase beats right, away from the lesion, and the patient leans or falls toward the left, the side of the lesion.

blocks.text: Taste receptor cells sit in taste buds on the fungiform papillae of the anterior tongue, the foliate papillae on its sides, and the circumvallate papillae just in front of the sulcus terminalis, with a few on the epiglottis and pharynx. They are modified epithelial cells, replaced from basal cells about every 10 days. Sweet, umami, and bitter tastes act on G protein coupled receptors that release Ca2+ through the IP3 pathway, open TRPM5 channels, and release ATP as the transmitter. Salt depolarizes the cell through Na+ entry by epithelial Na+ channels, and sour through H+ entry.

The anterior two thirds of the tongue sends taste in the chorda tympani branch of CN VII, which runs with the lingual nerve and then crosses the middle ear; its cell bodies lie in the geniculate ganglion. The posterior third, including the circumvallate papillae even though they lie in front of the sulcus, sends taste in CN IX, and the epiglottis in CN X. All three end in the rostral part of the nucleus of the solitary tract, which projects to the ipsilateral ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM) of the thalamus and then to the gustatory cortex in the anterior insula and frontal operculum. Touch and pain from the anterior tongue travel separately in the lingual nerve of CN V3, so a chorda tympani lesion removes taste but not sensation.

Olfactory receptor neurons are bipolar neurons in the epithelium of the nasal roof, replaced throughout life from basal stem cells. Each expresses one of several hundred odorant receptor types, all coupled to the G protein Golf. Odorant binding activates adenylyl cyclase, cAMP opens cyclic nucleotide-gated cation channels, and Ca2+ entering through them opens Ca2+-activated Cl- channels; because these neurons hold a high internal Cl-, Cl- leaves and adds to the depolarization.

Their thin unmyelinated axons pass in bundles through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone as the olfactory nerve (CN I) and synapse in glomeruli of the olfactory bulb, where all neurons expressing the same receptor converge. Mitral and tufted cells project through the olfactory tract and lateral olfactory stria directly to the piriform cortex, the amygdala, and the entorhinal cortex. Smell is the only sense that reaches its primary cortex without a thalamic relay, and its direct limbic links help explain the ties between odor, emotion, and memory.

Head trauma can shear the olfactory fila where they cross the cribriform plate, causing anosmia; a fracture that tears the dura also lets CSF leak from the nose (CSF rhinorrhea) and opens a route for meningitis. Anosmia also occurs with viral upper respiratory infections, early Parkinson and Alzheimer disease, and Kallmann syndrome, in which GnRH neurons fail to migrate with the olfactory axons, giving anosmia with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Because flavor depends largely on retronasal smell, patients with anosmia often complain that they have lost their sense of taste.

blocks.title: Taste and smell compared
rows: CN VII (anterior two thirds), IX (posterior third), X (epiglottis)
CN I through the cribriform plate
Piriform cortex, with amygdala and entorhinal cortex
Chorda tympani or facial nerve injury
blocks.caption: Taste follows the usual brainstem to thalamus to cortex sequence; smell bypasses the thalamus.

integration.text: Anatomy and physiology meet at the same few junctions. Crossing at the chiasm, bilateral pretectal projections, bilateral auditory relays above the cochlear nuclei, and two vestibular labyrinths compared against each other explain why vision gives homonymous defects, why an afferent pupil lesion never causes anisocoria, why cortical lesions do not cause one-sided deafness, and why one failed labyrinth produces vertigo. The facial nerve ties several senses together: tearing, the stapedius reflex, and taste leave it at successive levels, so testing them localizes a CN VII lesion.

Biochemistry and pathology explain the failures. Phototransduction and olfaction use cyclic nucleotide cascades, hair cells use a K+ gradient built by the stria vascularis, and the eye depends on vitamin A for both rhodopsin and healthy conjunctival epithelium. Tumors (pituitary adenoma, schwannoma of CN VIII), vascular disease (MCA and PCA strokes), infection (neurosyphilis, viral neuritis), trauma (cribriform fracture), and genetic disease (Kallmann syndrome) each strike a predictable point. These pathways are simplified: real lesions are often partial, and bedside tests such as tuning forks screen rather than measure.

summary: Nasal retinal fibers cross at the chiasm, so lesions in front of it are monocular, at it bitemporal, and behind it homonymous.
The Meyer loop in the temporal lobe carries the upper field and parietal radiations the lower field; PCA stroke gives hemianopia with macular sparing.
The light reflex runs CN II to the pretectal nucleus to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei to CN III, so an afferent lesion gives a relative afferent pupillary defect, never anisocoria.
Horner syndrome gives a small pupil, compressive CN III palsy a large one, and the Argyll Robertson pupil of neurosyphilis reacts to near but not to light.
Light isomerizes 11-cis retinal, transducin activates phosphodiesterase, cGMP falls, cation channels close, and the photoreceptor hyperpolarizes and releases less glutamate.
Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness first because rods depend on regenerated rhodopsin, then xerophthalmia from epithelial keratinization.
Ciliary epithelium secretes aqueous humor that drains through the trabecular meshwork and canal of Schlemm; tears come from meibomian (lipid), lacrimal (aqueous, CN VII), and goblet cells (mucin).
Hair cells depolarize by K+ entry from +80 mV endolymph; the cochlear base senses high and the apex low frequencies.
Weber lateralizes to a conductive ear and away from a sensorineural ear; Rinne is negative (bone louder than air) in conductive loss.
Canals sense angular and otoliths linear acceleration; unilateral vestibular loss gives nystagmus beating away from the lesion, and taste relays in the thalamus while smell does not.

verify: The tendency of pituitary adenomas to take the upper temporal fields first and craniopharyngiomas the lower temporal fields first is a pattern, not a rule; confirm how NABNE frames it.
The exact site of the Argyll Robertson lesion (pretectal region versus rostral midbrain near the Edinger-Westphal nucleus) is debated; this chapter gives the common teaching.

The share of aqueous outflow through the uveoscleral route is quoted from about 10% to more than 30% depending on age and source, and the upper limit of normal intraocular pressure is given as 20 or 21 mmHg.

Hair cell numbers (about 3,500 inner and 12,000 outer), the middle ear pressure gain (about 17 times area and 1.3 times lever), and the endocochlear potential (about +80 mV) vary slightly between texts.
The sour taste channel is identified as the proton channel otopetrin 1 (OTOP1) in recent work; older texts describe H+ entry through ENaC or H+ block of K+ channels. Confirm what NABNE expects.
Taste receptor cell turnover (about 10 days) and olfactory neuron replacement times differ between references.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Meyer loop, Marcus Gunn pupil, Argyll Robertson pupil, Edinger-Westphal nucleus, Heschl gyrus, and the COWS mnemonic.
